compression.title: MIT AI Incident Tracker
compression.lede: is the MIT AI Risk Initiative's machine classification of AI Incident Database reports by risk domain, cause, harm, severity and EU AI Act level, through Arcola AI's LLM pipeline (MMRS record; its page), its patterns, by its own word, "indicative".

sentences.text: The MIT AI Incident Tracker is a machine classification of AI Incident Database reports by risk domain, cause, harm, severity and EU AI Act risk level, made by Arcola AI's language-model pipeline against the MIT Risk Repository's taxonomy, and filed as a database (MMRS record); the MIT AI Risk Initiative's about page calls it "a catalogue that classifies incidents where AI has already caused harm", developed in collaboration with the AI Incident Database, and its own page says it classifies AIID incidents "by risk, cause, harm, severity, and other relevant dimensions".

It is derived from the AI Incident Database (MMRS record): the tracker page builds on the Responsible AI Collaborative, "who created and maintain the AI Incident Database, reviewing all submitted reports", and sends its readers to the AIID for how incidents are defined and ingested, and the about page lists the AIID among the users of the Initiative's work, mapping real-world incidents to its taxonomy in the tracker.

Its occasion, on its own page, is that incident databases "struggle with inconsistent structure, limiting their utility for policymaking", and its answer is a tool to classify incidents by risk and harm severity, offered as a common frame of reference for researchers, developers, businesses, evaluators, auditors, policymakers and regulators; the MMRS record restates the aim as a more consistent structure for AIID's records "by its own account", and the June 2026 update grounds it in what incident reporting did for safety in aviation, healthcare and nuclear power.

Raw AIID reports are "processed by Arcola AI's LLM pipeline", which categorizes them with the MIT Risk Repository and a harm severity rating based on CSET's AI Harm Taxonomy (tracker page); the June 2026 update says the tracker uses LLMs to classify incident reports along five taxonomies, "producing standardized data", the Navigator that each incident is classified against shared taxonomies "using an LLM pipeline with human spot-checking", and the MMRS record that the classification is machine-made, its intake the AIID reports passed through Arcola AI's pipeline.

The five taxonomies are harm severity across ten harm types, the EU AI Act risk tier, a causal taxonomy of lifecycle stage and intent, seven risk domains and twenty-four subdomains (June 2026 update); the tracker page shows each incident under the repository's causal and domain taxonomies and the EU AI Act's levels, with its severity across ten CSET-based harm categories and the classification's confidence, and the Initiative's home page lets incidents be compared by risk domain, harm, people affected, alleged developer, time or national-security impact.

On 23 June 2025 the severity scale went from 0–10 to 1–5, its definitions disambiguated in the first person ("I have tried to remove ambiguities"), and the tracker added flags for ambiguities and alternative interpretations and the system's primary goal by a taxonomy based on the AIID's GMF (June 2025 update).

A national-security view grades each incident's impact on its primary target country in five categories, from physical security and critical infrastructure to societal stability and human rights, with the threat classified for imminence, novelty and autonomy (tracker page; June 2025 update).

It is part of the MIT AI Risk Initiative (tracker page), based at MIT FutureTech, a joint initiative of MIT's Institute of the Digital Economy and CSAIL, which keeps several connected workstreams because no single dataset captures AI risk and presents its data and frameworks as authoritative (about and home pages; card 2's summary lists among its tools an expert survey and the AI Risk Repository); the MMRS record gives the operator as the Initiative "with Arcola AI's LLM pipeline" and the tracker as part of the MIT AI Risk Repository.

Simon Mylius "developed and leads the AI Incident Tracker", a classification tool and dashboard now hosted by the MIT AI Risk Repository, its analysis featured on the AIID (about page), and the tracker page's team names MIT FutureTech and University of Queensland researchers beside the AIID's Sean McGregor.

The MMRS record gives the unit as the AIID report, classified by domain, cause, harm, severity and EU AI Act level; the tracker's pages count incidents ("1,600 real-world report incidents"), and the June 2025 update reclassified "all incidents" up to AIID incident ID #1116.

MIT's surfaces give four figures: 1,600 in the tracker page's heading and "more than 1,400" in its description, which the MMRS record reports as the page giving its size twice; 1,752 "real-world AI incident reports" in the card's summary of that page; and on the Navigator "more than 1300" in its card and 1,497 in its page heading on 2026-10-29, beside headline figures of "Up -76%" year over year and 64% caused by AI systems.

The MMRS record's count field (as of 2026-10-28, basis observed) carries the page's two figures, Google's card's 1,752 and the Navigator's "more than 1300", each with its surface, and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records the count "three ways" and that the composition gave none.

The tracker is versioned by reclassification: the June 2025 update brought it up to AIID incident #1116 and classified the full dataset again with the new iteration "to ensure consistency", and the June 2026 update names as its next step a more comprehensive validation study and announces that the full set of AIID reports will be reclassified with the updated model selection and prompts.

That update (30 June 2026) reports a pilot: because the tracker relies on automated classification rather than manual review, two expert reviewers classified ten AIID incidents on the five taxonomies, eight LLMs were set against their consensus, and the human agreement was itself only "Fair" for harm severity (0.31) and "Moderate" for the EU AI Act level (0.56).

Opus 4.6 and Kimi K2.5 met or exceeded the model in current use, Sonnet 4, on most taxonomies, the models did substantially worse on the EU AI Act level, and after prompt refinement Opus 4.6 met the human baseline on all five "on this pilot sample", a sample the update calls small; it concludes that LLM classification has accuracy comparable to the human baseline.

The tracker page states its limits: the classification database explores "the potential capabilities and limitations of a scalable incident analysis framework", its AIID input rests on public and expert submissions of varying quality, voluntary reporting gives "some degree of sampling bias", spot-checks have improved it but "a systematic validation study has not yet been completed", and patterns "should be taken as indicative and validated through further analysis".

The June 2026 update adds that LLMs can hallucinate details and show a score-range bias, the Navigator calls itself a research prototype whose data and analyses are "preliminary and not yet validated", and the MMRS record carries the page's caveat in its kernel, its article and its note.

At its name Google's AI Overview composed the tracker "as what it says it is, with its machine method named", AIID as the source and LLM pipelines as the method, which are the MMRS record's derivation and intake, avoided stating a count, and left out the page's caveat of indicative patterns, voluntary reporting and no completed validation study (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
Data from the MIT AI Risk Initiative is licensed under CC BY 4.0 (tracker page), as most of its outputs are (about page).

In the MMRS record it is a derived layer, "the editor-resolved incidents of AIID, reclassified by a model", whose admission inherits AIID's harm test and whose classifications are machine-written, so that original outputs are not preserved, and the chain from event to news report to AIID record to machine classification is "a chain of receptions, each recorded".
The record keeps each assertion with its source and basis and the lifecycle apart from the observation that saw it (read 2026-10-28), and it rests every field on the one tracker page.

The June 2026 update places the tracker among the incident databases it builds on, the AI Incident Database, the OECD's AI Incident Monitor, the AIAAIC Repository and the Political Deepfakes Database, adding to them a classification of each incident and a rating of its harm; the MMRS record gives it the role of harm.
Its outputs have been used to report incident trends in the 2026 World Disasters Report and Time magazine (June 2026 update).

Wikipedia has no article for the tracker, nor for the AI Risk Repository or the MIT AI Risk Initiative, and none of its articles contains the phrase "AI Incident Tracker"; its one mention of the work, in "Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal", says that "The MIT AI Risk Repository catalogued the incident" as "economic and cultural devaluation of human effort", referenced to the AIID's page for incident 277, which on 2026-10-29 shows the MIT classification as machine-classified under subdomain 4.3, fraud, scams and targeted manipulation, in the domain Malicious Actors & Misuse.
